signs: Physical examination is frequently NORMAL between attacks, and a normal examination never excludes the diagnosis. During an episode there may be tachycardia, a rise in blood pressure, a fourth heart sound, a transient apical systolic murmur of ischaemic mitral regurgitation, and basal crackles. Look for evidence of atherosclerosis and risk factors - arcus senilis and xanthelasma, tendon xanthomata, carotid and femoral bruits, reduced peripheral pulses, hypertension, central obesity and diabetic changes on fundoscopy

anaemia, thyrotoxicosis and aortic stenosis (a slow-rising pulse with an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids) can precipitate or mimic angina. A RESTING ECG is normal in about half of patients but may show ST depression, T-wave inversion, pathological Q waves from prior infarction or left ventricular hypertrophy. Confirm with exercise ECG (ST depression of 1 mm or more that is horizontal or downsloping), stress echocardiography, myocardial perfusion imaging or CT coronary angiography, with invasive coronary angiography where revascularisation is contemplated. Grade severity by the Canadian Cardiovascular Society classification I to IV

Also refer immediately: prolonged chest pain unrelieved by rest or three doses of sublingual nitrate

signs: The patient is typically anxious, restless, pale, sweating and cool peripherally. Tachycardia (or BRADYCARDIA and hypotension in inferior/right ventricular infarction with vagal activation)
blood pressure may be raised, normal or low
low-grade fever after 12-24 hours
a fourth heart sound is almost always present, a third heart sound indicates significant left ventricular dysfunction

a new apical pansystolic murmur suggests ischaemic MITRAL REGURGITATION from papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture, and a new harsh pansystolic murmur with a thrill suggests VENTRICULAR SEPTAL RUPTURE
a pericardial friction rub may appear after 2-3 days

basal crackles and raised JVP in heart failure - grade by the Killip classification I to IV. ST depression or T-wave inversion in NSTEMI

localise the territory - II, III and aVF inferior (right coronary), V1-V4 anteroseptal (left anterior descending), I, aVL and V5-V6 lateral (circumflex), with tall R waves and ST depression in V1-V2 for posterior infarction

always record right-sided leads V3R-V4R in inferior infarction. Cardiac TROPONIN I or T rises within 3-4 hours, peaks at 24 hours and remains elevated for 7-14 days - a rise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th percentile, together with ischaemic symptoms, ECG changes or imaging evidence, defines myocardial infarction (Fourth Universal Definition). Echocardiography shows regional wall motion abnormality

INVESTIGATIONS: raised BNP or NT-proBNP is the key rule-out test (a normal level makes untreated heart failure very unlikely)

signs: Assess the pulse rate, rhythm, volume and character
an IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR pulse with a pulse deficit (apex rate exceeding radial rate) indicates ATRIAL FIBRILLATION
a regular rapid pulse of 150/min suggests atrial flutter with 2:1 block
cannon A waves in the jugular venous pulse indicate atrioventricular dissociation (ventricular tachycardia or complete heart block)

variable intensity of the first heart sound also indicates AV dissociation. Assess haemodynamic stability - blood pressure, level of consciousness, peripheral perfusion, chest pain and signs of heart failure. Examine for underlying causes: thyrotoxicosis (goitre, tremor, lid lag), valvular disease (especially mitral stenosis in atrial fibrillation), heart failure, anaemia and alcohol excess. THE 12-LEAD ECG DURING SYMPTOMS IS THE DEFINITIVE INVESTIGATION - assess rate, regularity, P-wave presence and relationship to QRS, and QRS width: narrow-complex regular (sinus tachycardia, atrial flutter, AVNRT, AVRT), narrow-complex irregular (atrial fibrillation, multifocal atrial tachycardia), broad-complex regular (ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise, or SVT with aberrancy), broad-complex irregular (atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block or pre-excitation, polymorphic VT/torsades). Look for a delta wave and short PR interval (Wolff-Parkinson-White), a prolonged QTc, Brugada-type ST elevation in V1-V3, epsilon waves, and evidence of prior infarction. Ambulatory Holter or event monitoring for intermittent symptoms
echocardiography for structural disease
check electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium), thyroid function, full blood count and drug levels

Also emergency: broad-complex tachycardia (treat as VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA)
polymorphic VT/torsades de pointes with a prolonged QT (stop the offending drug, give magnesium)
ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest (immediate defibrillation and CPR)

a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40

signs: ACUTE RHEUMATIC FEVER is diagnosed by the REVISED JONES CRITERIA - two major, or one major and two minor manifestations, plus evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection (raised or rising ASO or anti-DNase B titre, positive throat culture or rapid antigen test). MAJOR: carditis (clinical or subclinical on echocardiography), polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum (a pink, non-pruritic, serpiginous macular rash with central clearing on the trunk and proximal limbs, sparing the face), and subcutaneous nodules (firm, painless, mobile, 0.5-2 cm over extensor surfaces and bony prominences). MINOR: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR or CRP, and a prolonged PR interval. CHRONIC RHEUMATIC VALVULAR DISEASE - MITRAL STENOSIS: a tapping, non-displaced apex beat, a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with presystolic accentuation at the apex, best heard in the left lateral position with the bell, a malar flush, atrial fibrillation with an irregularly irregular pulse, a loud P2 and right ventricular heave with pulmonary hypertension. MITRAL REGURGITATION: a displaced hyperdynamic apex, a soft first sound, a third heart sound and a blowing pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. AORTIC REGURGITATION: a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, wide pulse pressure, a displaced heaving apex and an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge on leaning forward in expiration, with an Austin Flint murmur, plus Corrigan's, de Musset's, Quincke's, Traube's and Duroziez's signs. AORTIC STENOSIS: a slow-rising low-volume pulse, narrow pulse pressure, a heaving undisplaced apex and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids with a soft or absent A2. ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY is diagnostic and grades severity
ECG shows P mitrale, atrial fibrillation, LVH or right ventricular hypertrophy
chest radiograph shows left atrial enlargement with a double right heart border, splaying of the carina, a straightened left heart border and pulmonary venous congestion or valve calcification

redFlags: Acute pulmonary oedema or severe breathlessness at rest
haemoptysis, especially massive
new atrial fibrillation with fast ventricular rate and haemodynamic compromise (anticoagulate - the embolic risk in rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF is very high)
systemic embolism causing stroke or acute limb ischaemia

signs: Rapid recognition using FAST - Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Full neurological examination: level of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale)
higher functions and language (fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming)
cranial nerves including visual fields, conjugate gaze deviation TOWARDS the side of the lesion in hemispheric stroke, and pupillary responses
UPPER MOTOR NEURON pattern of weakness with initial flaccidity progressing to spasticity, hyperreflexia and an EXTENSOR PLANTAR RESPONSE
sensory loss
cerebellar signs

and gait. Localise the territory - ANTERIOR CEREBRAL ARTERY: contralateral leg-predominant weakness with sensory loss and urinary incontinence. MIDDLE CEREBRAL ARTERY: contralateral face and arm-predominant weakness and sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, gaze deviation, with dysphasia if the dominant hemisphere is involved and neglect if the non-dominant. POSTERIOR CIRCULATION: vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia, crossed sensory findings and cortical blindness. LACUNAR: pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis or clumsy-hand dysarthria without cortical signs. Score severity with the NIHSS. Check pulse for ATRIAL FIBRILLATION, blood pressure in both arms, carotid bruits, heart murmurs, fundoscopy for hypertensive or embolic changes, and CAPILLARY BLOOD GLUCOSE IMMEDIATELY (hypoglycaemia is the great mimic). URGENT NON-CONTRAST CT BRAIN is required first to exclude haemorrhage
early ischaemic signs include loss of grey-white differentiation, insular ribbon sign, a hyperdense MCA sign and sulcal effacement, while infarct hypodensity may not appear for hours
MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging detects ischaemia within minutes
CT or MR angiography identifies large vessel occlusion

redFlags: STROKE IS A TIME-CRITICAL EMERGENCY - 'TIME IS BRAIN'. Activate the stroke pathway and transfer immediately to a stroke unit: intravenous thrombolysis is indicated within 4.5 hours of onset and mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion up to 24 hours in selected patients. Check glucose and obtain non-contrast CT before any thrombolysis. Danger signs requiring critical care: reduced or declining level of consciousness
a large MCA territory infarct with midline shift (malignant MCA syndrome - consider decompressive craniectomy)
cerebellar infarct with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus
basilar artery occlusion (fluctuating consciousness, quadriparesis, cranial nerve palsies - very high mortality)
seizures
respiratory compromise or failure to protect the airway
hypoglycaemia (correct immediately). Also urgent: any transient ischaemic attack (up to 10% risk of stroke within a week - assess and treat immediately, do not defer)
stroke in a young patient (investigate for dissection, patent foramen ovale, vasculitis, thrombophilia and drug use)
atrial fibrillation (anticoagulate after the appropriate interval)
carotid stenosis of 50-99% on the symptomatic side (endarterectomy within 2 weeks)
NIL BY MOUTH until a formal SWALLOW SCREEN is done (aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death)
avoid lowering blood pressure aggressively in acute ischaemic stroke unless thrombolysis is planned or it exceeds 220/120 mmHg

signs: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT DISTINCTION IS UPPER VERSUS LOWER MOTOR NEURON. In LOWER MOTOR NEURON (peripheral) palsy - Bell's palsy, Ramsay Hunt, otitis media, parotid tumour, trauma - THE WHOLE HALF OF THE FACE INCLUDING THE FOREHEAD IS PARALYSED: the patient cannot wrinkle the forehead or raise the eyebrow on the affected side. In UPPER MOTOR NEURON palsy (stroke or other supranuclear lesion) THE FOREHEAD IS SPARED because of bilateral cortical innervation of the upper face, and emotional (spontaneous) smiling may be preserved while voluntary movement is lost. Test each branch: raise the eyebrows (frontalis), close the eyes tightly against resistance (orbicularis oculi), show the teeth and smile (zygomaticus and buccinator), purse the lips and whistle, blow out the cheeks, and tense the neck (platysma). Look for BELL'S PHENOMENON - upward rolling of the globe on attempted eye closure, with incomplete lid closure and a visible sclera. Grade severity by the HOUSE-BRACKMANN scale I to VI. Examine the EAR AND MASTOID CAREFULLY - otoscopy for otitis media, cholesteatoma or a discharging ear, and inspect the pinna, external canal, palate and anterior tongue for the VESICLES of RAMSAY HUNT SYNDROME (herpes zoster oticus, which also causes vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss). Palpate the PAROTID GLAND for a mass. Test taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, corneal sensation and the corneal reflex, hearing with tuning forks, and ALL OTHER CRANIAL NERVES

signs: ASSESS VOLUME STATUS FIRST, as this determines management: in HYPOVOLAEMIA there is tachycardia, postural or frank HYPOTENSION, a low jugular venous pressure, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, delayed capillary refill, cool peripheries and concentrated urine

Examine for signs of sepsis, an abdominal aortic aneurysm, abdominal compartment syndrome, a renal bruit, and rash or livedo reticularis (vasculitis, cholesterol emboli)

signs: ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION for a palpable, dull, percussible suprapubic mass arising out of the pelvis (a distended bladder in chronic retention - it cannot be got below). DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION IS ESSENTIAL and in benign hyperplasia reveals a SMOOTH, SYMMETRICALLY ENLARGED, FIRM-BUT-ELASTIC (rubbery) prostate with a PRESERVED MEDIAN SULCUS and intact mobile overlying rectal mucosa - in contrast to CARCINOMA, which is HARD, NODULAR, IRREGULAR AND ASYMMETRICAL with LOSS OF THE MEDIAN SULCUS, and possibly fixed with extension beyond the capsule. Assess anal tone and perineal sensation to exclude a neurological cause. Examine the external genitalia for meatal stenosis and phimosis. Quantify symptoms with the INTERNATIONAL PROSTATE SYMPTOM SCORE (IPSS) - mild 0-7, moderate 8-19, severe 20-35 - together with the quality-of-life question. Ask the patient to complete a FREQUENCY-VOLUME CHART for 3 days. INVESTIGATIONS: urinalysis and culture to exclude infection and haematuria

signs: In ACUTE BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS the patient is febrile, tachycardic and unwell, with suprapubic tenderness and sometimes a palpable distended bladder. DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION reveals an EXQUISITELY TENDER, HOT, SWOLLEN AND BOGGY PROSTATE - and VIGOROUS PROSTATIC MASSAGE MUST BE AVOIDED IN THE ACUTE PHASE because it is intensely painful and may precipitate bacteraemia. In CHRONIC PROSTATITIS the prostate may feel normal, mildly tender, or boggy, and there is often tenderness of the pelvic floor musculature, the levator ani and the coccyx, with palpable myofascial trigger points. Examine the external genitalia and epididymes to exclude epididymo-orchitis, and the abdomen for a distended bladder. INVESTIGATIONS: urinalysis, MIDSTREAM URINE MICROSCOPY AND CULTURE, and BLOOD CULTURES in the acute form
full blood count showing leucocytosis, and raised CRP
a markedly RAISED PSA is common in acute prostatitis and should NOT be measured during the acute episode, nor interpreted as cancer - repeat it at least 4-6 weeks after resolution
NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in younger, sexually active men
the MEARES-STAMEY FOUR-GLASS TEST or the simpler two-glass pre- and post-massage test localises infection to the prostate in the chronic bacterial form
measure post-void residual volume
transrectal ultrasound or CT if abscess is suspected
use the NIH-CHRONIC PROSTATITIS SYMPTOM INDEX to quantify symptoms and monitor response

signs: The patient may appear well or show signs of DEHYDRATION - dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, tachycardia, postural hypotension and a low jugular venous pressure - particularly if thirst is impaired or water is unavailable. Assess for visual field defects by confrontation (BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA from a suprasellar lesion compressing the optic chiasm), cranial nerve palsies, and features of hypopituitarism
examine growth and development in children. INVESTIGATIONS: confirm true polyuria with a 24-HOUR URINE VOLUME above 3 litres (or 40-50 mL/kg)

simultaneous serum and urine osmolality shows a LOW URINE OSMOLALITY (typically below 300 mOsm/kg and often below 200) with a HIGH-NORMAL OR RAISED SERUM OSMOLALITY (above 295 mOsm/kg) and a serum SODIUM at the upper limit or frankly raised - the combination of hypernatraemia with dilute urine is virtually diagnostic

in primary polydipsia the serum sodium and osmolality are LOW. THE WATER DEPRIVATION TEST WITH DESMOPRESSIN remains the classical confirmatory test and MUST BE PERFORMED UNDER CLOSE SUPERVISION WITH HOURLY WEIGHT, OSMOLALITY AND SODIUM MONITORING, and stopped if weight falls by more than 3-5%: in normal subjects and primary polydipsia the urine concentrates above 750 mOsm/kg
in CENTRAL diabetes insipidus the urine remains dilute after deprivation but CONCENTRATES BY MORE THAN 50% AFTER DESMOPRESSIN

in NEPHROGENIC disease it fails to concentrate after both. Measurement of COPEPTIN, particularly after arginine or hypertonic saline stimulation, has now largely superseded the water deprivation test where available. Also check calcium, potassium, glucose (to exclude diabetes mellitus, the far commoner cause of polyuria), renal function, and lithium levels

MRI OF THE PITUITARY AND HYPOTHALAMUS is mandatory in central disease and characteristically shows LOSS OF THE NORMAL POSTERIOR PITUITARY BRIGHT SPOT on T1-weighted imaging, and may reveal a tumour, thickened stalk or infiltrative lesion
assess full anterior pituitary function

redFlags: SEVERE HYPERNATRAEMIA AND HYPOVOLAEMIC SHOCK if fluid intake is interrupted - this is the principal danger, and it arises whenever thirst or access to water is impaired: in the UNCONSCIOUS PATIENT, the very young, the elderly, those with hypothalamic damage causing ADIPSIA, patients who are nil by mouth, and perioperatively. Such patients can lose litres of urine per hour and become critically hypernatraemic within hours - they require hourly monitoring of urine output, sodium and osmolality with meticulous fluid replacement. Note also that CORRECTING HYPERNATRAEMIA TOO RAPIDLY RISKS CEREBRAL OEDEMA, so lower the sodium by no more than 10-12 mmol/L in 24 hours. Other red flags: new-onset diabetes insipidus with HEADACHE AND VISUAL FIELD LOSS (suprasellar mass - urgent MRI and neurosurgical referral)
diabetes insipidus after head injury or pituitary surgery, which may follow a TRIPHASIC pattern of DI, then SIADH, then permanent DI (monitor sodium closely)

associated anterior pituitary hormone deficiency, particularly ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY, which must be treated first - CORTISOL DEFICIENCY CAN MASK DIABETES INSIPIDUS, so polyuria may appear or worsen only after starting hydrocortisone
diabetes insipidus in pregnancy (transient gestational DI from placental vasopressinase, and an association with pre-eclampsia and acute fatty liver)
hypercalcaemia or lithium toxicity as a cause (review the drug with the prescribing psychiatrist - lithium-induced nephrogenic DI may be irreversible)
diabetes insipidus in a child with growth failure (exclude craniopharyngioma and histiocytosis)
and never confuse it with DIABETES MELLITUS - always check the blood glucose first in any patient with polyuria and polydipsia

SMOOTH, TENDER HEPATOMEGALY in the majority
mild SPLENOMEGALY in about 10-20%
posterior cervical lymphadenopathy
scratch marks in cholestatic disease
low-grade fever
bradycardia may accompany deep jaundice

the urine is dark (conjugated bilirubinuria) and the stools pale. IMPORTANTLY, THERE ARE NO STIGMATA OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE - no spider naevi, palmar erythema, clubbing, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, ascites or caput medusae - and their presence should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. LABORATORY: MARKEDLY RAISED TRANSAMINASES, typically 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal with ALT USUALLY EXCEEDING AST (values of 1000-3000 IU/L are common and peak just before or as jaundice appears)
raised conjugated and unconjugated BILIRUBIN
alkaline phosphatase is normal or only modestly raised except in the cholestatic variant
PROTHROMBIN TIME/INR IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT PROGNOSTIC TEST and should be checked in every patient
albumin is normal in acute disease

there may be a mild leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis. ASTERIXIS (flapping tremor)
a PROLONGED PROTHROMBIN TIME OR INR ABOVE 1.5 NOT CORRECTED BY VITAMIN K
hypoglycaemia
a rapidly SHRINKING LIVER with falling transaminases and rising bilirubin (an ominous combination)

bleeding
and this constitutes a medical emergency requiring urgent referral to a liver transplant centre. Also refer or admit: persistent vomiting with inability to maintain hydration

signs: ACUTE: jaundice, tender smooth hepatomegaly, occasional splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, urticarial rash and arthritis in the prodrome

transaminases in the thousands with ALT above AST, raised bilirubin, and an INR that must be monitored. CHRONIC HEPATITIS AND CIRRHOSIS: examine specifically for the STIGMATA OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE - spider naevi in the distribution of the superior vena cava, palmar erythema, leuconychia, clubbing, Dupuytren's contracture, gynaecomastia, loss of body hair, testicular atrophy, parotid enlargement, jaundice, scratch marks, easy bruising, a firm irregular liver edge or a small shrunken liver, SPLENOMEGALY and other signs of PORTAL HYPERTENSION including ascites with shifting dullness and a fluid thrill, caput medusae and dilated abdominal veins with flow away from the umbilicus

in DECOMPENSATION, look for ASTERIXIS, fetor hepaticus, confusion and altered sleep pattern (encephalopathy), peripheral oedema and muscle wasting. SEROLOGY IS THE KEY TO INTERPRETATION: HBsAg positive indicates current infection, and PERSISTENCE BEYOND 6 MONTHS DEFINES CHRONIC INFECTION
anti-HBc IgM indicates acute or recent infection
anti-HBc IgG indicates past exposure
HBeAg indicates high replication and high infectivity
anti-HBe suggests seroconversion to a lower replicative state, although HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis with precore mutants remains active

likewise, NEVER STOP ANTIVIRAL THERAPY ABRUPTLY, which can precipitate a severe flare. a sudden ALT flare
coinfection with HEPATITIS D, which markedly worsens prognosis

PREGNANCY - screen every pregnant woman, give ANTIVIRAL THERAPY IN THE THIRD TRIMESTER for high viral load, and ensure the neonate receives HEPATITIS B IMMUNOGLOBULIN AND THE FIRST VACCINE DOSE WITHIN 12 HOURS OF BIRTH, which prevents the great majority of perinatal transmission
needle-stick exposure (give immunoglobulin and vaccine promptly)
and vaccinate all household and sexual contacts

signs: EXAMINATION IS OFTEN COMPLETELY NORMAL in chronic hepatitis C, which is precisely why screening of at-risk groups matters. When present, findings are those of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension - spider naevi, palmar erythema, leuconychia, clubbing, Dupuytren's contracture, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, jaundice, a firm irregular or shrunken liver, SPLENOMEGALY, ascites with shifting dullness, caput medusae, peripheral oedema, asterixis and confusion in decompensation. Look for extrahepatic signs - PALPABLE PURPURA over the lower limbs and livedo, with peripheral neuropathy (cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis)
blistering, milia, scarring and hypertrichosis on the dorsa of the hands (porphyria cutanea tarda)

violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules with Wickham striae, and oral lacy white lesions (lichen planus). LABORATORY: ALT is often only MILDLY RAISED AND FLUCTUATES, and MAY BE PERSISTENTLY NORMAL IN UP TO A THIRD OF PATIENTS DESPITE SIGNIFICANT FIBROSIS - so a normal ALT never excludes hepatitis C or advanced disease. SCREEN WITH ANTI-HCV ANTIBODY, and CONFIRM ACTIVE INFECTION WITH HCV RNA BY PCR, because antibody persists after spontaneous or treatment-induced clearance
determine the GENOTYPE where it affects regimen choice. Assess FIBROSIS STAGE non-invasively with TRANSIENT ELASTOGRAPHY (FibroScan), APRI or FIB-4 scores, or by biopsy where necessary

check full blood count for thrombocytopenia, albumin, bilirubin, INR, alpha-fetoprotein, ultrasound, cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor and complement (low C4) where vasculitis is suspected, and TEST FOR HIV AND HEPATITIS B COINFECTION
screen for diabetes and assess alcohol intake, since alcohol markedly accelerates fibrosis

spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

PREGNANCY (DAAs are not currently recommended
test the infant after 18 months)
renal impairment requiring regimen adjustment
DRUG INTERACTIONS with DAAs, which are extensive and must be checked (amiodarone with sofosbuvir can cause severe bradycardia)
and ADVISE COMPLETE ALCOHOL ABSTINENCE, vaccinate against hepatitis A and B, and address injecting-drug harm reduction and reinfection risk

signs: Findings mirror those of severe acute or chronic hepatitis B - jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and splenomegaly in the acute phase, with the STIGMATA OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE AND PORTAL HYPERTENSION (spider naevi, palmar erythema, clubbing, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, a firm irregular or shrunken liver, splenomegaly, ascites, caput medusae, oedema, asterixis and encephalopathy) appearing EARLIER AND PROGRESSING FASTER than in HBV monoinfection. LABORATORY: markedly raised transaminases, often BIPHASIC in coinfection
raised bilirubin

and in advanced disease a falling albumin, rising INR and thrombocytopenia. DIAGNOSIS: SCREEN EVERY HBsAg-POSITIVE PERSON AT LEAST ONCE FOR HDV with TOTAL ANTI-HDV ANTIBODY, and CONFIRM ACTIVE INFECTION WITH HDV RNA BY PCR (anti-HDV IgM indicates active replication)

HDAg can be detected in serum early and in liver tissue. DISTINGUISHING COINFECTION FROM SUPERINFECTION MATTERS FOR PROGNOSIS: in COINFECTION, ANTI-HBc IgM IS POSITIVE (indicating simultaneous acute HBV), the course is usually self-limiting and chronicity is uncommon at under 5%

signs: INSPECTION WITH GENTLE PARTING OF THE BUTTOCKS IS USUALLY DIAGNOSTIC AND IS ALL THAT IS REQUIRED - a longitudinal, linear or pear-shaped ulcer in the ANODERM. OVER 90% ARE LOCATED IN THE POSTERIOR MIDLINE, with about 10% anterior (commoner in women after childbirth). An ACUTE fissure appears as a fresh, sharply demarcated superficial tear with clean edges. A CHRONIC fissure shows the triad of INDURATED EVERTED EDGES with the exposed WHITE HORIZONTAL FIBRES OF THE INTERNAL ANAL SPHINCTER VISIBLE IN THE BASE, a SENTINEL SKIN TAG at the distal (external) end, and a HYPERTROPHIED ANAL PAPILLA at the proximal (internal) end. There is marked internal sphincter HYPERTONIA AND SPASM, which is central to the pathophysiology - the raised resting anal pressure causes ischaemia of the posterior commissure, which is the least well perfused part of the anal canal, and prevents healing. DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION AND PROCTOSCOPY ARE EXTREMELY PAINFUL AND SHOULD BE DEFERRED in a typical acute fissure until the pain has settled or examination is performed under anaesthesia
do not force them. Note that a fissure that is LATERAL in position, MULTIPLE, IRREGULAR, PAINLESS, BROAD-BASED OR UNDERMINED IS ATYPICAL and demands investigation for an underlying cause

and recurrent fissures. MANAGEMENT PRINCIPLES: the cornerstone is to BREAK THE CYCLE by softening the stool and relaxing the sphincter - a high-fibre diet with 25-30 g daily, ample fluids, bulk-forming laxatives or osmotic agents such as lactulose or macrogol, and avoidance of straining and prolonged sitting

and TOPICAL GLYCERYL TRINITRATE 0.2-0.4% OR DILTIAZEM 2% APPLIED TWICE DAILY FOR 6-8 WEEKS as chemical sphincterotomy - warn the patient that GTN commonly causes HEADACHE, which is the main reason for discontinuation, and that diltiazem is better tolerated

signs: First establish that the sound is truly wheeze and not STRIDOR, which is a harsh predominantly INSPIRATORY sound loudest over the NECK indicating EXTRATHORACIC UPPER AIRWAY obstruction and is a far more urgent finding. GENERALISED, BILATERAL, POLYPHONIC EXPIRATORY WHEEZE with a prolonged expiratory phase indicates diffuse small airway narrowing as in asthma and COPD. A FIXED, LOCALISED, MONOPHONIC WHEEZE THAT DOES NOT CLEAR WITH COUGHING INDICATES OBSTRUCTION OF A SINGLE LARGE AIRWAY and must be investigated for TUMOUR, FOREIGN BODY, or extrinsic compression by node or mass. Assess: respiratory rate, ability to speak in full sentences, use of ACCESSORY MUSCLES, intercostal, subcostal and suprasternal RECESSION, tracheal tug, nasal flaring and grunting in children, cyanosis, level of consciousness, pulse rate, PULSUS PARADOXUS, OXYGEN SATURATION and PEAK EXPIRATORY FLOW RATE
hyperinflation with a barrel chest, hyperresonance and reduced breath sounds

urticaria, angioedema and hypotension (anaphylaxis)
clubbing and copious sputum (bronchiectasis)

lymphadenopathy and weight loss (malignancy). and bronchoscopy for a persistent localised wheeze

signs: MEASURE THE TEMPERATURE ACCURATELY AND CONSISTENTLY BY ROUTE, and record the pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, capillary refill and level of consciousness. Look for RELATIVE BRADYCARDIA (typhoid, brucellosis, legionella, dengue) or disproportionate tachycardia. UNDERTAKE A SYSTEMATIC HEAD-TO-TOE SEARCH FOR A FOCUS: throat and tonsils, ears and mastoids, sinuses, teeth and gums
neck stiffness, Kernig and Brudzinski signs and the fundi for papilloedema
lymph nodes at all sites
chest for consolidation and effusion

abdomen for tenderness, guarding, organomegaly and renal angle tenderness
SKIN FOR RASH - and in particular for a NON-BLANCHING PETECHIAL OR PURPURIC RASH, which demands immediate action

calves for deep vein thrombosis
perineum, genitalia and rectum
all indwelling lines, catheters and surgical wounds

and pressure areas. INVESTIGATIONS guided by the assessment: full blood count with differential (neutrophilia in bacterial infection, LEUCOPENIA WITH LYMPHOCYTOSIS in typhoid, dengue and many viral infections, EOSINOPHILIA in parasitic and allergic disease), CRP and procalcitonin, blood cultures (at least two sets before antibiotics), urinalysis and culture, MALARIA THICK AND THIN FILMS OR RAPID TEST IN ANYONE WITH RELEVANT TRAVEL, chest radiograph, renal and liver function, dengue NS1 and serology, typhoid blood culture, HIV test, and further imaging, lumbar puncture, echocardiography or biopsy as indicated. FEVER OF UNKNOWN ORIGIN is defined as a temperature above 38.3C on several occasions for more than 3 weeks with no diagnosis after appropriate initial investigation, and its major causes are infection, malignancy (especially lymphoma and renal cell carcinoma), connective tissue and inflammatory disease, and drugs

signs: Physical examination is usually entirely NORMAL

there may be mild abdominal tenderness, and in a minority some weight loss. DIAGNOSIS: examination of the STOOL and of PROGLOTTIDS is central - the SPECIES IS DISTINGUISHED BY COUNTING THE PRIMARY LATERAL UTERINE BRANCHES OF A GRAVID PROGLOTTID cleared or injected with India ink: TAENIA SAGINATA HAS 15-30 BRANCHES ON EACH SIDE, WHILE TAENIA SOLIUM HAS ONLY 7-13 - AND THIS DISTINCTION IS OF MAJOR CLINICAL IMPORTANCE, since T. solium carries the risk of cysticercosis for the patient and for household contacts. The SCOLEX also differs - T. saginata has four suckers and NO hooklets, whereas T. SOLIUM HAS FOUR SUCKERS AND A ROSTELLUM ARMED WITH A DOUBLE ROW OF HOOKLETS ('ARMED' TAPEWORM). THE EGGS OF THE TWO SPECIES ARE MORPHOLOGICALLY IDENTICAL - brown, spherical, 30-40 micrometres, with a thick radially striated shell containing a six-hooked oncosphere - SO EGGS ALONE CANNOT SPECIATE THE INFECTION
the perianal cellophane tape swab increases egg detection for T. saginata
stool PCR and coproantigen ELISA give species-specific diagnosis where available. Peripheral EOSINOPHILIA is mild or absent in intestinal taeniasis

redFlags: THE CRITICAL RED FLAG IS IDENTIFICATION OF TAENIA SOLIUM, BECAUSE OF THE RISK OF CYSTICERCOSIS AND NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS: a T. solium carrier is a danger to themselves and to their household, and every such case requires prompt treatment, careful hand and food hygiene education, and SCREENING OF HOUSEHOLD CONTACTS FOR BOTH TAENIASIS AND CYSTICERCOSIS. Refer or investigate urgently: NEW-ONSET SEIZURES, headache, focal neurological deficit or raised intracranial pressure in a person with taeniasis or from an endemic area (NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS - image the brain BEFORE treating, since anthelmintic-induced destruction of cysts provokes intense inflammation and can precipitate seizures, cerebral oedema and, with intraventricular cysts, acute hydrocephalus
treatment must be given with corticosteroid and anticonvulsant cover under specialist supervision)

visual disturbance or eye pain (OCULAR CYSTICERCOSIS - ALWAYS EXAMINE THE FUNDI AND EXCLUDE INTRAOCULAR CYSTS BEFORE GIVING ANTHELMINTICS, since inflammation around a dying intraocular cyst can destroy vision)
subcutaneous nodules

and in DIPHYLLOBOTHRIUM latum infection (the fish tapeworm, an important differential) MEGALOBLASTIC ANAEMIA FROM VITAMIN B12 DEFICIENCY. Other considerations: intestinal obstruction, appendicitis or biliary obstruction from migrating proglottids are rare but reported

PRAZIQUANTEL (single dose) OR NICLOSAMIDE is curative for intestinal taeniasis, and a purgative may be given to recover the scolex and confirm cure - note that PRAZIQUANTEL SHOULD BE USED WITH CAUTION IN A PATIENT WHO MAY HAVE NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS. PREVENTION AND PUBLIC HEALTH: taeniasis is preventable by THOROUGH COOKING OF BEEF AND PORK to at least 63C or freezing at -10C for several days, meat inspection and condemnation of infected carcasses, improved pig husbandry with confinement of pigs away from human faeces, SANITATION AND SAFE DISPOSAL OF HUMAN FAECES, hand washing, safe water and health education
T. solium is a WHO-listed neglected tropical disease targeted for control through combined human and porcine interventions

signs: GENERAL EXAMINATION may reveal firm, painless, mobile SUBCUTANEOUS NODULES 0.5-2 cm in diameter over the trunk, arms and thighs, which can be biopsied for definitive diagnosis. NEUROLOGICAL examination varies from entirely normal (common in parenchymal disease presenting only with seizures) to focal deficits, cranial nerve palsies, cerebellar signs, papilloedema and reduced consciousness. FUNDOSCOPY IS MANDATORY IN EVERY SUSPECTED CASE, BOTH FOR PAPILLOEDEMA AND TO IDENTIFY AN INTRAOCULAR CYST, since giving anthelmintic therapy in the presence of an untreated ocular cyst can cause severe inflammation and blindness. IMAGING IS THE CORNERSTONE OF DIAGNOSIS: CT is excellent for demonstrating CALCIFIED lesions, which appear as small punctate calcifications, while MRI IS SUPERIOR for viable cysts, for cysts in the ventricles, basal cisterns, brainstem and spinal cord, and for showing perilesional oedema
the classical appearance is a small round CYSTIC LESION CONTAINING AN ECCENTRIC HYPERDENSE MURAL NODULE - THE SCOLEX - which gives the pathognomonic 'HOLE-WITH-DOT' OR 'STARRY SKY' APPEARANCE
lesions are staged as VESICULAR (viable, no enhancement or oedema), COLLOIDAL VESICULAR (degenerating, ring-enhancing with surrounding oedema), GRANULAR NODULAR, and finally CALCIFIED (dead)

muscle radiographs may show characteristic 'RICE GRAIN' or cigar-shaped calcifications. SEROLOGY by ENZYME-LINKED IMMUNOELECTROTRANSFER BLOT (EITB) using lentil lectin-purified glycoprotein antigens is far more specific than ELISA, though it is INSENSITIVE IN SINGLE-LESION AND CALCIFIED-ONLY DISEASE
CSF may show lymphocytic pleocytosis with EOSINOPHILS, raised protein and LOW GLUCOSE in subarachnoid disease
DEL BRUTTO'S REVISED DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA combine absolute, major, minor and epidemiological criteria
ALWAYS EXAMINE THE STOOL OF THE PATIENT AND OF HOUSEHOLD MEMBERS FOR TAENIA EGGS AND PROGLOTTIDS

redFlags: TREATMENT MUST BE INDIVIDUALISED AND IS NOT ALWAYS ANTHELMINTIC - THE MOST IMPORTANT PRINCIPLE IS THAT KILLING CYSTS RELEASES ANTIGEN AND PROVOKES AN INTENSE INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE THAT CAN BE MORE DANGEROUS THAN THE INFECTION ITSELF. EMERGENCIES AND CONTRAINDICATIONS: RAISED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE OR HYDROCEPHALUS - reduced consciousness, papilloedema, vomiting, bradycardia and hypertension - REQUIRES URGENT NEUROSURGICAL DECOMPRESSION OR SHUNTING AND CORTICOSTEROIDS, AND ANTHELMINTIC THERAPY MUST NOT BE GIVEN UNTIL THE PRESSURE IS CONTROLLED, since it can precipitate fatal deterioration
OCULAR CYSTICERCOSIS MUST BE EXCLUDED BY FUNDOSCOPY BEFORE TREATMENT, and intraocular cysts are managed surgically, not medically

CYSTICERCOTIC ENCEPHALITIS with numerous inflamed cysts and diffuse cerebral oedema, seen particularly in children and young women, is a CONTRAINDICATION to anthelmintic therapy and requires steroids and pressure control
SUBARACHNOID (RACEMOSE) DISEASE in the basal cisterns and giant cysts carry a poor prognosis and need prolonged therapy under specialist care
SPINAL disease with cord compression requires urgent surgical assessment

and STATUS EPILEPTICUS requires standard emergency management. GENERAL PRINCIPLES: give ALBENDAZOLE (with praziquantel added for multiple cysts) ALWAYS UNDER CORTICOSTEROID COVER AND WITH ANTIEPILEPTIC DRUGS, in a specialist setting
CALCIFIED LESIONS ALONE REPRESENT DEAD PARASITES AND SHOULD NOT BE TREATED WITH ANTHELMINTICS - they require antiepileptic therapy only
treat any coexisting intestinal taeniasis. PUBLIC HEALTH: SCREEN AND TREAT HOUSEHOLD CONTACTS FOR TAENIASIS, as the carrier is the source
emphasise hand washing, safe water, washing of vegetables, sanitation and the safe disposal of human faeces, pig confinement, meat inspection and thorough cooking of pork

signs: Examine for LYMPHOEDEMA and stage it: Grade 1 - pitting oedema that reverses on elevation
Grade 2 - non-pitting oedema that does not reverse on elevation

Grade 3 (ELEPHANTIASIS) - gross, non-pitting swelling with THICKENED, HYPERKERATOTIC, VERRUCOUS ('MOSSY') SKIN, deep folds, fissuring and ulceration, most often of the LOWER LIMB but also the arm, breast and genitalia. The LEG SWELLING OF FILARIASIS CHARACTERISTICALLY INVOLVES THE FOOT AND TOES with a squared-off appearance and a positive STEMMER SIGN (inability to pinch a fold of skin at the base of the second toe), which helps distinguish lymphoedema from venous or cardiac oedema. HYDROCELE - a non-tender, fluctuant scrotal swelling that TRANSILLUMINATES BRILLIANTLY and in which one CANNOT GET ABOVE THE SWELLING is the commonest chronic manifestation of bancroftian filariasis

examine also for lymph scrotum with dilated cutaneous lymphatics oozing lymph. During acute attacks: fever, tender enlarged inguinal or axillary nodes with a cord-like tender lymphatic tracking DOWNWARD from the node, and overlying erythema and warmth (distinguish ACUTE DERMATOLYMPHANGIOADENITIS, which is bacterial and follows entry through skin cracks, from true acute filarial lymphangitis). DIAGNOSIS: demonstration of MICROFILARIAE ON A THICK BLOOD FILM, and CRUCIALLY THE SAMPLE MUST BE TAKEN AT NIGHT, USUALLY BETWEEN 10 p.m. AND 2 a.m., BECAUSE OF THE NOCTURNAL PERIODICITY OF W. BANCROFTI AND B. MALAYI (a daytime sample will commonly be falsely negative) - concentration techniques such as membrane filtration or Knott's method increase yield
the RAPID CIRCULATING FILARIAL ANTIGEN TEST (ICT card or FTS) for W. bancrofti can be performed AT ANY TIME OF DAY and is the preferred field diagnostic

redFlags: REFER OR ACT URGENTLY: recurrent ACUTE BACTERIAL DERMATOLYMPHANGIOADENITIS with high fever, spreading cellulitis and systemic toxicity - this needs antibiotics and is the principal driver of progression of lymphoedema, so its PREVENTION THROUGH RIGOROUS FOOT AND SKIN HYGIENE IS THE SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE INTERVENTION IN CHRONIC DISEASE
ulceration, deep fissuring or necrosis of an oedematous limb
a large or complicated hydrocele causing pain or disability (surgery is curative and transformative for quality of life)
CHYLURIA with weight loss and hypoproteinaemia
acute scrotal pain (exclude TESTICULAR TORSION and epididymo-orchitis)

and TROPICAL PULMONARY EOSINOPHILIA, which if untreated progresses to irreversible pulmonary FIBROSIS and which responds dramatically to diethylcarbamazine - so it must be actively considered in any patient from an endemic area with nocturnal asthma and eosinophilia. IMPORTANT TREATMENT CAUTIONS: DIETHYLCARBAMAZINE (DEC) MUST NOT BE GIVEN IF ONCHOCERCIASIS IS POSSIBLE, BECAUSE IT PRECIPITATES A SEVERE MAZZOTTI REACTION AND CAN CAUSE BLINDNESS, AND IT SHOULD BE AVOIDED IN LOA LOA CO-INFECTION WITH HIGH MICROFILARIAL LOADS BECAUSE OF THE RISK OF FATAL ENCEPHALOPATHY - so in areas where these are co-endemic, alternative regimens (ivermectin plus albendazole, or albendazole alone) are used
systemic reactions to treatment (fever, headache, myalgia, nausea) reflect dying microfilariae and are commoner with high parasite loads

DOXYCYCLINE for 4-6 weeks targets the endosymbiotic WOLBACHIA bacteria, has macrofilaricidal activity and improves lymphoedema. CHRONIC CARE: lymphoedema is NOT reversed by antifilarial drugs, and MORBIDITY MANAGEMENT AND DISABILITY PREVENTION is the mainstay - daily washing with soap and water, drying carefully between the toes, treating entry lesions and interdigital fungal infection, wearing protective footwear, elevation, exercise and compression where appropriate. PUBLIC HEALTH: lymphatic filariasis is a WHO-targeted NEGLECTED TROPICAL DISEASE for elimination through annual MASS DRUG ADMINISTRATION to entire at-risk populations, combined with vector control and morbidity management

conditions.firstLine: TREATMENT of mild/moderate anaemia (Hb 7-10.9 g/dl): 3 mg of elemental iron per kg per day for 2 months. IFA syrup age bands - children 6-12 months (6-10.9 kg) 1 ml once a day; 1-3 years (11-14.9 kg) 1.5 ml once a day; 3-5 years (15-19.9 kg) 2 ml once a day. Re-check haemoglobin after 2 months; if normalised, stop treatment and continue the PROPHYLACTIC dose. Hb below 7 g/dl is severe anaemia - refer urgently, do not manage at this level. PROPHYLAXIS (Table 4): children 6-59 months biweekly 1 ml IFA syrup (20 mg elemental iron + 100 mcg folic acid per ml); children 5-9 years weekly 1 tablet (45 mg elemental iron + 400 mcg folic acid, pink); adolescents 10-19 years weekly 1 tablet (60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid, blue); women of reproductive age 20-49 weekly 1 tablet (60 mg + 500 mcg, red); pregnant and lactating women daily 1 tablet (60 mg + 500 mcg, red) from the fourth month of pregnancy, minimum 180 days in pregnancy and 180 days post-partum. Withhold prophylaxis during acute illness and in thalassaemia major. All women pre-conception and in the first trimester should take 400 mcg folic acid daily to reduce neural tube defects. Deworming is part of the anaemia strategy - see the helminth entries.

signs: ASSESS DEPTH: SUPERFICIAL (epidermal, first-degree) - erythema, dry, painful, blanches on pressure, no blisters, heals in 5-7 days without scarring
SUPERFICIAL PARTIAL-THICKNESS (superficial dermal) - blisters, moist, pink, VERY painful, brisk capillary refill, heals in 2-3 weeks with minimal scarring
DEEP PARTIAL-THICKNESS (deep dermal) - blotchy red or white, less painful, sluggish or absent capillary refill, reduced sensation, heals slowly with scarring and often needs grafting
FULL-THICKNESS (third-degree) - dry, leathery, waxy white, brown or charred, INSENSATE, no capillary refill, thrombosed vessels visible, requires grafting

FOURTH-DEGREE involves fascia, muscle or bone. ESTIMATE TOTAL BODY SURFACE AREA using the WALLACE RULE OF NINES in adults - head and neck 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, front of trunk 18%, back of trunk 18%, perineum 1% - MODIFIED IN CHILDREN, whose head is proportionately larger (use the LUND AND BROWDER CHART, which is the most accurate at all ages)
the patient's PALM WITH FINGERS approximates 1% for small or patchy burns

DO NOT INCLUDE SIMPLE ERYTHEMA in the TBSA calculation. ASSESS FOR INHALATION INJURY: burns to the face and neck, singed nasal hairs and eyebrows, soot in the nostrils, mouth or sputum, hoarseness, stridor, brassy cough, respiratory distress, and a history of a fire in an enclosed space - and measure carboxyhaemoglobin, remembering that PULSE OXIMETRY IS FALSELY NORMAL IN CARBON MONOXIDE POISONING. Check circumferential burns of the limbs, digits, neck or chest for distal pulses, capillary refill and chest expansion (ESCHAR causing compartment syndrome). Calculate fluid requirements by the PARKLAND FORMULA - 4 mL x body weight in kg x %TBSA of Ringer's lactate in the first 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours FROM THE TIME OF INJURY, titrated to a urine output of 0.5-1 mL/kg/h in adults and 1-1.5 mL/kg/h in children

give high-flow oxygen for suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, and consider CYANIDE toxicity in fires involving plastics. REFER TO A SPECIALIST BURNS UNIT: burns over 10% TBSA in adults or over 5% in children

CHEMICAL, ELECTRICAL (including all high-voltage and lightning injuries, which cause deep tissue damage, RHABDOMYOLYSIS with myoglobinuric renal failure and CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIAS requiring ECG monitoring) and inhalation injuries

and any burn where NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY OR ABUSE is suspected (mandatory safeguarding referral). Estimate the percentage of total body surface area burned and the depth. Cover with a clean non-adherent dressing. Do NOT apply toothpaste, oil, butter or other traditional remedies. Refer urgently for burns that are extensive, deep, circumferential, or involve the face, hands, feet, perineum or joints, and for any inhalation injury or electrical burn. Fluid resuscitation and analgesia are needed for significant burns and require their own sourced protocols. Assess tetanus immunisation status.

signs: The CLASSICAL SIGNS OF FRACTURE are PAIN AND TENDERNESS LOCALISED OVER THE BONE, SWELLING, DEFORMITY (angulation, rotation or shortening), LOSS OF FUNCTION, ABNORMAL MOBILITY and CREPITUS - the last two should NOT be deliberately elicited, as they cause severe pain and further soft tissue and neurovascular damage. Examine and document: the overlying SKIN, to determine whether the fracture is CLOSED or OPEN (compound), since any wound communicating with the fracture changes management entirely
LIMB ALIGNMENT, LENGTH AND ROTATION

and, most importantly, THE NEUROVASCULAR STATUS DISTAL TO THE INJURY BEFORE AND AFTER ANY MANIPULATION OR SPLINTING - palpate distal pulses, assess capillary refill, skin colour and temperature, and test motor and sensory function of each relevant nerve. Examine the JOINT ABOVE AND THE JOINT BELOW, as associated injuries and dislocations are frequently missed. Assess for associated injuries and, in high-energy trauma, follow the ATLS primary survey. RADIOGRAPHY should include TWO VIEWS AT RIGHT ANGLES (AP and lateral) AND INCLUDE THE JOINT ABOVE AND BELOW
use decision rules such as the OTTAWA ANKLE AND KNEE RULES to guide imaging

note that some fractures are RADIOGRAPHICALLY OCCULT INITIALLY - particularly the SCAPHOID (tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox with a normal film should be splinted and re-imaged or investigated with MRI, since missed scaphoid fracture leads to avascular necrosis and non-union), the femoral neck, and stress fractures - and CT or MRI may be needed. Describe fractures systematically by site, pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental, impacted, avulsion, greenstick), displacement, angulation, rotation, shortening, intra-articular extension and whether open or closed

redFlags: IMMEDIATE ORTHOPAEDIC AND SURGICAL EMERGENCIES: OPEN (COMPOUND) FRACTURE - any wound over a fracture requires urgent intravenous ANTIBIOTICS, TETANUS PROPHYLAXIS, removal of gross contamination, a sterile saline-soaked dressing, splinting, photography of the wound and URGENT SURGICAL DEBRIDEMENT, since infection and osteomyelitis are the principal risks. NEUROVASCULAR COMPROMISE - an absent or diminished distal pulse, a pale cold pulseless limb, or a new neurological deficit requires IMMEDIATE reduction of the deformity and urgent vascular assessment

classic associations include brachial artery injury in supracondylar humeral fracture in children, popliteal artery injury in knee dislocation and proximal tibial fracture, and sciatic nerve injury in posterior hip dislocation. COMPARTMENT SYNDROME - the cardinal early feature is PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION TO THE INJURY AND PAIN ON PASSIVE STRETCHING OF THE MUSCLES IN THE COMPARTMENT, together with a tense swollen compartment, paraesthesia and, only very late, pulselessness and paralysis - THE PRESENCE OF A PALPABLE PULSE DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT, and it demands IMMEDIATE removal of all circumferential dressings and casts and URGENT FASCIOTOMY, since delay causes irreversible muscle necrosis and Volkmann's contracture. Other red flags: HIP FRACTURE in an older person (a shortened, externally rotated limb - needs prompt surgery, as delay increases mortality, along with assessment of the cause of the fall and osteoporosis treatment)
SPINAL FRACTURE with neurological deficit, or any suspicion of spinal injury (immobilise and image before moving)
PELVIC FRACTURE with haemodynamic instability (major haemorrhage - apply a pelvic binder)
FEMORAL SHAFT FRACTURE (significant blood loss and FAT EMBOLISM SYNDROME, which presents 24-72 hours later with hypoxia, confusion and a petechial rash)
dislocation (reduce urgently to avoid avascular necrosis, especially of the hip and shoulder)
MULTIPLE RIB FRACTURES AND FLAIL CHEST (respiratory compromise and pulmonary contusion)
suspected pathological fracture (investigate for malignancy and myeloma)
SUSPECTED NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY IN A CHILD (mandatory safeguarding referral and skeletal survey)
and any fragility fracture, which should trigger osteoporosis assessment and treatment to prevent the next one
conditions.firstLine: Immobilisation and referral, not a drug regimen. Assess neurovascular status distal to the injury BEFORE and AFTER immobilisation. Immobilise the joint above and below. Do not attempt reduction without imaging and appropriate skills. Cover any open wound with a sterile dressing - an open fracture is a surgical emergency requiring urgent referral, tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics. Refer for radiography and definitive orthopaedic management. Analgesia is needed but requires its own sourced regimen and is not encoded here.

check ANKLE REFLEXES

a deep fissure with exposed subcutaneous tissue or bleeding
a fissure that PROBES TO BONE (osteomyelitis)
black necrotic tissue or gangrene
absent pedal pulses or an ABPI below 0.9 (peripheral arterial disease - refer to vascular services)
loss of protective sensation
a non-healing heel lesion, which may be a PRESSURE ULCER in an immobile or bed-bound patient (heels are the second commonest site of pressure ulceration and require offloading with heel protectors)

and cracked heels with generalised dry skin, fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance (CHECK THYROID FUNCTION). MANAGEMENT: soak and gently debride the callus with a pumice or foot file (NEVER cut it with a blade at home, and never in a diabetic)

use a thick occlusive ointment at night under cotton socks
treat any coexisting tinea
wear closed, well-fitting, cushioned footwear with a firm heel counter and avoid barefoot walking
maintain hydration and manage obesity
and treat the underlying dermatosis or systemic cause
conditions.firstLine: Skin care, not a drug regimen. Soak the feet and gently debride thickened callus. Apply an emollient regularly, particularly after bathing. Advise well-fitting closed footwear and avoiding prolonged barefoot walking. Screen for underlying causes - DIABETES in particular, where a heel fissure can become an entry point for infection, and also hypothyroidism and vitamin deficiency. Refer any fissure that is infected, deep, or occurring in a person with diabetes or peripheral vascular disease.

conditions.firstLine: PREFERRED: 5% permethrin cream. Children 2 months and over and adults - one application with a contact time of 8 hours, then rinse thoroughly; REPEAT the application after 7 days. Apply over the ENTIRE body including scalp, post-auricular areas, umbilicus, palms and soles, avoiding mucous membranes, the face, and the breasts in breastfeeding women. Do not shorten or exceed the contact time. The patient must not wash their hands while the product is on (or must reapply if they do). conditions.firstLine: MOST CASES ARE VIRAL AND NEED NO ANTIBIOTIC. Symptomatic treatment for fever and pain: paracetamol or ibuprofen PO. Use the CENTOR SCORE: a score under 2 rules out group A streptococcus - no antibiotic. Score 2 or more, or scarlet fever - give antibiotic to prevent acute rheumatic fever. In patients with immunosuppression or a personal or family history of ARF, do NOT use the Centor score - treat empirically. FIRST CHOICE where single-use injection equipment is available: benzathine benzylpenicillin IM as a SINGLE dose - children under 30 kg (or under 10 years) 600,000 IU; children 30 kg and over (or 10 years and over) and adults 1.2 MIU. It is the only antibiotic proven to reduce rheumatic fever incidence. ORAL REFERENCE: phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) PO for 10 days - under 1 year 125 mg twice daily; 1 to under 6 years 250 mg twice daily; 6 to under 12 years 500 mg twice daily; 12 years and over and adults 1 g twice daily. Adherence is often poor because of the length. ALTERNATIVE: amoxicillin PO for 6 days - children 25 mg/kg twice daily, adults 1 g twice daily - but AVOID until infectious mononucleosis is excluded, as it causes adverse skin reactions in undiagnosed IM. PENICILLIN-ALLERGIC ONLY: azithromycin PO for 3 days - children 20 mg/kg once daily (max 500 mg), adults 500 mg once daily; macrolide resistance is frequent and efficacy in preventing rheumatic fever is unstudied.

conditions.firstLine: ACUTE ATTACK: salbutamol metered-dose inhaler 100 micrograms/puff - 2 to 10 puffs every 20 minutes during the FIRST HOUR. In children use a SPACER, with a face mask in children under 3 years; give single puffs one at a time and let the child breathe 4 to 5 times from the spacer before repeating. Add prednisolone PO as a single dose of 1 to 2 mg/kg (maximum 50 mg) for children over 5 years and adults. If the attack is only partially resolved, continue salbutamol MDI 2 to 10 puffs every 1 to 4 hours until symptoms subside; for children up to 5 years give one dose of prednisolone PO as above if symptoms persist. FOLLOW-ON: salbutamol MDI for 24 to 48 hours at 2 to 4 puffs every 4 to 6 hours depending on clinical evolution, plus prednisolone PO once daily at the same dose to complete 5 days of treatment. Reassess after 1 to 2 days: address any identified risk factor and reassess the need for salbutamol and for long-term controller therapy. SEVERE ATTACK with nebuliser available: salbutamol plus ipratropium nebuliser solutions with oxygen via nasal cannula during nebulisation - children under 5 years salbutamol 2.5 mg (1.25 ml) + ipratropium 0.25 mg (1 ml) every 20 minutes; children 5 to 11 years salbutamol 2.5 to 5 mg (1.25 to 2.5 ml) + ipratropium 0.5 mg (2 ml) every 20 minutes.

signs: DENGUE WITHOUT WARNING SIGNS: fever plus 2 of - nausea/vomiting; measles-like rash; generalised aches (headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia); benign mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, positive tourniquet test, epistaxis, gingival bleeding); leucopenia

WARNING SIGNS (any one): intense abdominal pain; persistent vomiting; fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion); mucosal bleeding; hepatomegaly over 2 cm; postural hypotension; agitation or lethargy; increasing haematocrit

SEVERE DENGUE: severe fluid accumulation with respiratory distress and/or shock; severe mucocutaneous bleeding; severe organ involvement (transaminases over 1000 IU/L, myocarditis, altered mental status)
TOURNIQUET TEST: inflate a BP cuff midway between systolic and diastolic for 5 minutes - positive if 20 or more petechiae per 2.5 cm square

conditions.firstLine: Place the patient under a MOSQUITO NET. Encourage oral fluid intake including ORS. AVOID INVASIVE PROCEDURES - no nasogastric tube, no IM injections - to minimise bleeding risk. Fever and pain: PARACETAMOL PO only, with caution and without exceeding children 10 mg/kg every 6 to 8 hours, adults 500 mg every 6 to 8 hours. IF TRANSAMINASES ARE MORE THAN 10 TIMES THE UPPER LIMIT OF NORMAL, DO NOT GIVE PARACETAMOL - use tepid sponging instead. NSAIDs are listed as a bleeding risk factor and must be avoided. Monitor vital signs, fluid intake and urine output every 4 hours. If oral intake is poor, give IV maintenance fluid - children 5% glucose + Ringer lactate by the Holliday-Segar formula (4 ml/kg/hour for the first 10 kg + 2 ml/kg/hour for the next 10 kg + 1 ml/kg/hour for each kg above 20); adults Ringer lactate 2 to 3 ml/kg/hour. IF WARNING SIGNS: monitor hourly for at least 4 hours, give a Ringer lactate bolus of 10 ml/kg over one hour (5 ml/kg over one hour if 65 and over or with co-morbidities), reassess, up to a maximum of 3 boluses; if no improvement after 3 boluses treat as severe dengue and transfer to intensive care.

conditions.firstLine: GENERAL PRINCIPLES: prevent or treat dehydration with prompt fluid and electrolyte replacement until the diarrhoea stops; give zinc sulfate to children under 5; prevent malnutrition; DO NOT give antimicrobials systematically - only certain diarrhoeas need them. BLOODY DIARRHOEA (dysentery): treat first as SHIGELLOSIS - ciprofloxacin PO for 3 days, children 15 mg/kg twice daily; use ceftriaxone IM 50 to 100 mg/kg once daily for 3 days if the infection is severe or oral administration is impossible. If resistant or contraindicated, or no improvement within 48 hours: azithromycin PO for 5 days (children 12 mg/kg on day 1 then 6 mg/kg once daily days 2-5) or cefixime PO 8 mg/kg once daily for 5 days (max 400 mg daily). If there is no improvement 48 hours after second-line treatment, TREAT FOR AMOEBIASIS. AMOEBIASIS confirmed on stool examination: tinidazole PO - children 50 mg/kg once daily for 3 days (max 2 g daily), adults 2 g once daily for 3 days; OR metronidazole PO - children 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days, adults 500 mg three times daily for 5 days. THE PRESENCE OF CYSTS ALONE SHOULD NOT LEAD TO TREATMENT FOR AMOEBIASIS. Amoebic liver abscess: same drugs, tinidazole for 5 days or metronidazole for 5 to 10 days.

conditions.firstLine: COUNSELLING IS THE BASE OF TREATMENT. Pharmacological treatment should ALWAYS be offered ALONGSIDE counselling in severe depression (PHQ-9 above 19, severe functional impairment, psychotic symptoms, or suicidal risk). In moderately severe depression (PHQ-9 15-19), consider medication if there is no improvement after 3 counselling sessions, or from the outset if the patient prefers it. BEFORE PRESCRIBING, make sure 9-month treatment and follow-up are possible. Prefer a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, particularly in older patients; prefer fluoxetine, except in PREGNANCY where sertraline is preferred. Fluoxetine PO 20 mg on ALTERNATE days for one week, then once daily for 3 weeks, then increase if necessary to a maximum of 40 mg daily - use with caution in severe anxiety or immobilised patients. OR paroxetine PO 10 mg once daily for 3 days, then 20 mg once daily for 3 weeks, then increase if needed to a maximum of 40 mg daily - especially if there is severe anxiety. OR sertraline PO 25 mg once daily for 3 days, then 50 mg once daily for 3 weeks, then increase if needed to a maximum of 100 mg daily. Assess tolerance and response WEEKLY for 4 weeks. If response is inadequate after 4 weeks at optimal dose, or the SRI is poorly tolerated, switch to another SRI - no medication-free interval is needed. If SRIs are unavailable, amitriptyline PO starting 25 mg once daily at bedtime, increasing gradually over 8 to 10 days to 75 mg once daily (max 150 mg daily); IN OLDER PATIENTS HALVE THE DOSE. THE THERAPEUTIC DOSE OF AMITRIPTYLINE IS CLOSE TO THE LETHAL DOSE. There is a delay of 2 to 3 weeks before an SRI takes effect, and at least 4 weeks for amitriptyline.

conditions.firstLine: Determine the source of the anxiety and reassure the patient WITHOUT minimising the distress. Use simple relaxation techniques - for hyperventilation, help the patient control their breathing rate in a comfortable position with eyes closed, guiding a cycle of inhale (count to three), exhale (count to three), pause (count to three). IF SYMPTOMS ARE EXACERBATED (tachycardia, feeling of suffocation, fear of dying or 'going crazy', agitation or prostration): diazepam 5 to 10 mg PO or 10 mg IM, repeated after one hour if required. ACUTE SEVERE ANXIETY may justify a short course of maximum 2 to 3 weeks: diazepam PO 2.5 to 5 mg twice daily, halving the dose in the last few days. MODERATE ANXIETY lasting more than 2 weeks, first-line: hydroxyzine PO 25 to 50 mg twice daily (maximum 100 mg daily); or, ONLY if there is no improvement after 1 week, diazepam PO 2.5 to 5 mg twice daily for a maximum of 2 weeks. IF SYMPTOMS RECUR AFTER STOPPING, DO NOT RESUME diazepam or hydroxyzine - re-evaluate for depression or PTSD. Generalised anxiety lasting more than 2 months and not improving with psychosocial intervention: an antidepressant - fluoxetine or paroxetine PO 20 mg once daily - continued for 2 to 3 months after symptoms resolve, then stopped gradually over 2 weeks.

conditions.firstLine: TREAT THE CAUSE, not the symptom. If insomnia is related to an organic cause, treat that cause - for example give analgesics for pain. If it is related to alcohol, drugs or a medication, management depends on the substance; the main drugs known to cause sleep problems are corticosteroids, beta blockers, levodopa/carbidopa, fluoxetine and levothyroxine. If it is related to a particular life event such as bereavement, a SHORT course of a sedative may be used: promethazine PO 25 mg once daily at bedtime for 7 to 10 days; or if promethazine is unavailable, hydroxyzine PO 25 mg once daily at bedtime for 7 to 10 days; or, AS A LAST RESORT because of addiction risk, diazepam PO 2 to 5 mg once daily at bedtime for a maximum of 7 days. IF INSOMNIA PERSISTS, re-evaluate the patient - insomnia is a common feature of depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and anxiety disorders, and in those cases the underlying disorder must be addressed rather than the sleep.

conditions.firstLine: COMMONLY USED ANALGESICS ARE OFTEN INEFFECTIVE for this type of pain. Treatment is based on a combination of two centrally acting drugs. AMITRIPTYLINE PO - adults 25 mg once daily at bedtime in week 1; 50 mg once daily at bedtime in week 2; 75 mg once daily at bedtime from week 3; maximum 150 mg daily. REDUCE THE DOSE BY HALF IN ELDERLY PATIENTS. CARBAMAZEPINE PO - adults 200 mg once daily at bedtime in week 1; 200 mg twice daily in week 2; 200 mg three times daily from week 3. GIVEN ITS TERATOGENIC RISK, carbamazepine should only be used in women of childbearing age when covered by effective contraception (intrauterine device or injectable progestogen), and is not recommended in pregnant women. Treat the underlying cause in parallel - diabetes, B12 deficiency, HIV, drug toxicity, leprosy.

conditions.firstLine: RULE OUT OTHER CAUSES before diagnosing functional uterine bleeding - pregnancy, a poorly tolerated contraceptive, endometrial cancer in postmenopausal women, cervical pathology, genitourinary schistosomiasis in endemic areas, vaginal infection or salpingitis. ACUTE HEAVY BLEEDING: tranexamic acid IV 10 mg/kg (max 600 mg) every 8 hours; once bleeding is reduced switch to tranexamic acid PO 1 g three times daily until bleeding stops, maximum 5 days. If bleeding persists or tranexamic acid is contraindicated, and there is NO suspicion of cervical or endometrial cancer, give one of: ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel PO (0.03 mg/0.15 mg tablet) one tablet three times daily for 7 days; or medroxyprogesterone acetate PO 20 mg three times daily for 7 days. ENLARGED IRREGULAR UTERUS (fibroids): surgical management is required if medical treatment fails; while waiting, treat as functional bleeding. NORMAL UTERUS AND CERVIX (functional uterine bleeding): tranexamic acid as above; for repeated bleeding it can be combined with an NSAID (ibuprofen PO for 3 to 5 days) and/or a long-term treatment - levonorgestrel intrauterine device, or ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel PO one tablet daily, or medroxyprogesterone acetate IM 150 mg every 3 months, or medroxyprogesterone acetate PO 10 mg once daily (up to 30 mg if necessary) for 21 days each month. Note that oral medroxyprogesterone, unlike the others, has NO contraceptive effect. Treat associated iron deficiency anaemia.

conditions.firstLine: COMBINATION THERAPY FOR 6 WEEKS - brucellosis is not treated with a single agent. CHILDREN UNDER 8 YEARS: co-trimoxazole + rifampicin, or co-trimoxazole + gentamicin. CHILDREN 8 YEARS AND OVER, AND ADULTS: doxycycline + rifampicin, or doxycycline + gentamicin. PREGNANT OR BREASTFEEDING WOMEN: rifampicin, or doxycycline + streptomycin or gentamicin. DOSES - co-trimoxazole PO for 6 weeks, children under 8 years 20 mg sulfamethoxazole + 4 mg trimethoprim per kg (max 800 mg SMX + 160 mg TMP) twice daily. Doxycycline PO for 6 weeks, children 8 years and under 45 kg 2 to 2.2 mg/kg (max 100 mg) twice daily, children 45 kg and adults 100 mg twice daily. Rifampicin PO for 6 weeks, children 15 to 20 mg/kg (max 600 mg) once daily, adults 600 to 900 mg once daily. Gentamicin IM for 2 weeks, children and adults 5 mg/kg once daily. Streptomycin IM for 2 weeks, adults 1 g once daily. FOR LOCALISED FORMS the same treatment is given for 6 weeks to 4 months depending on the form. PREVENTION: hand and clothing washing after animal contact; boil milk; avoid unpasteurised milk products; cook offal thoroughly.

signs: Warm, tender, swollen, well-demarcated erythematous plaque
Fever, lymphadenopathy and lymphangitis
LOOK FOR THE PORTAL OF ENTRY - bite, ulcer, wound, intertrigo, eczema, fungal infection
OUTLINE THE AREA OF ERYTHEMA WITH A PEN to track progression
Erysipelas is superficial (dermis and superficial lymphatics); cellulitis affects deeper dermis and subcutaneous fat
Risk factors: venous insufficiency, obesity, oedema or lymphoedema, previous episode, immunosuppression, cutaneous inflammation
tests: Clinical diagnosis
Ultrasound can detect cellulitis and rule out an underlying abscess, deep vein thrombosis or foreign body
Radiography can detect a foreign body, underlying osteomyelitis, or gas in the subcutaneous tissue - but ABSENCE of gas does NOT rule out necrotising infection
URINE DIPSTICK FOR PROTEINURIA 3 WEEKS AFTER the infection to look for glomerulonephritis
redFlags: NECROTISING FASCIITIS - intense pain disproportionate to the skin lesion, hypoesthesia, rapidly progressing local signs, crepitus, skin necrosis, or a critically ill appearance. This is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY
Septicaemia
Acute glomerulonephritis
Osteomyelitis or septic arthritis
Orbital or periorbital involvement - a separate pathway
Worsening clinical signs after 48 hours of antibiotics
referralCriteria: Suspected necrotising fasciitis, septic arthritis or osteomyelitis - URGENT transfer to a surgical centre, starting antibiotics while awaiting transfer
HOSPITALISE: children under 3 months; critically ill appearance; local complications; debilitated patients (chronic conditions, elderly); risk of non-compliance or treatment failure
Worsening after 48 hours of oral antibiotics - consider IV route
conditions.firstLine: IN ALL CASES: outline the area of erythema with a pen to follow the infection. Bed rest and elevation of the affected area. Treat the pain - but AVOID NSAIDs, which may increase the risk of necrotising fasciitis. Treat the portal of entry and any comorbidity. CHECK AND CATCH UP TETANUS VACCINATION. OUTPATIENT ANTIBIOTICS: cefalexin PO for 7 to 10 days - children 1 month to under 12 years 25 mg/kg twice daily; children 12 years and over and adults 1 g twice daily. OR amoxicillin/clavulanic acid PO for 7 to 10 days using an 8:1 or 7:1 formulation, dose expressed as amoxicillin - children under 40 kg 25 mg/kg twice daily; children 40 kg and adults 2000 mg daily as 2 tablets of 500/62.5 mg twice daily (8:1 ratio) or 1750 mg daily as 1 tablet of 875/125 mg twice daily (7:1 ratio). If clinical signs worsen after 48 hours of antibiotic treatment, consider the IV route. HOSPITALISE children under 3 months, critically ill or debilitated patients, those with local complications, and those at risk of non-compliance or treatment failure.

notes: AVOID NSAIDs - MSF states they may increase the risk of necrotising fasciitis. This is a hard instruction, not a caution, and matters because NSAIDs are the reflex analgesic for a painful red limb.
Outlining the erythema with a pen is the practical way to detect progression between reviews - it is encoded as a sign rather than buried in prose.
Check proteinuria 3 weeks after the infection to detect post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Tetanus vaccination status must be checked - the portal of entry is usually a wound.
